{{Short description|Function which measures the "size" of elements in a field or integral domain}}
{{About|a generalization of the concept|a narrower mathematical sense of [[Magnitude (mathematics)#Numbers|magnitude]]|Absolute value||Absolute value (disambiguation)}}

In [[algebra]], an '''absolute value'''{{efn|''[[valuation (disambiguation)#Mathematics|Valuation]]'', ''[[norm (mathematics)|norm]]'' and ''[[magnitude (mathematics)|magnitude]]'' are related concepts that must not be confused with the subject of this article, although they may coincide in some cases. For example, an absolute value is a norm, but norms are defined on vector spaces, and a [[field norm]] is generally not an absolute value. A valuation is often the logarithm of an absolute value. "Magnitude" may be considered as a synonym of absolute value only in the usual real and complex cases. }} is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] that generalizes the usual [[absolute value]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Koblitz |first=Neal |authorlink=Neal Koblitz |title=P-adic numbers, p-adic analysis, and zeta-functions |edition=2nd |year=1984 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-96017-3 |url=https://www.springer.com/mathematics/numbers/book/978-0-387-96017-3 |accessdate=24 August 2012 |page=1 |quote=The metrics we'll be dealing with will come from ''norms'' on the field ''F''...}}</ref> More precisely, if {{math|''D''}} is a [[field (mathematics)|field]] or (more generally) an [[integral domain]], an ''absolute value'' on {{math|''D''}} is a function, commonly denoted <math>|x|,</math> from {{math|''D''}} to the [[real number]]s  satisfying:
{|
|-
| style="width:1.1em" | || style="width:.8em" | •|| <math>\left|x\right|\geq0</math> || style="width:3em" | || (non-negativity)
|-
| ||•|| <math>\left|x\right|=0</math> if and only if <math>x=0</math> || || ([[Positive-definite function|positive definiteness]])
|-
| ||•|| <math>\left|xy\right|=\left|x\right|\left|y\right|</math> || || (multiplicativity)
|-
| ||•|| <math>\left|x+y\right|\leq\left|x\right|+\left|y\right|</math> || || ([[triangle inequality]])
|}

It follows from the axioms that <math>|1| = 1,</math>  <math>|-1| = 1,</math> and <math>|-x|=|x|</math> for every {{tmath|x}}. Furthermore, for every positive [[integer]] {{math|''n''}},
<math>|n|\le n,</math> where the leftmost {{mvar|n}} denotes the sum of {{mvar|n}} summands equal to the [[identity element]] of {{mvar|D}}.

The classical [[absolute value]] and its [[square root]] are examples of absolute values, but the square of the classical absolute value is not, as it does not fulfill the triangular inequality.

An absolute value induces a [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] (and thus a [[Topological space#Definitions|topology]]) on {{math|''D''}} by setting <math>d(x,y) = |x - y|.</math>

== Examples ==
*The standard absolute value on the integers, the rationals and the real numbers: <math>|x|=x</math> for <math>x\geq 0</math> and <math>|x|=-x</math> for <math>x<0</math>.
*The standard [[Absolute value#Complex numbers|absolute value]] or modulus on the [[complex numbers]]: <math>|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}</math> for <math>a,b\in\mathbb{R}</math>.
*The [[P-adic valuation#p-adic absolute value|''p''-adic absolute value]] on the [[rational numbers]], where ''p'' is a fixed [[Prime number|prime]]: <math>|0|_p=0</math> and for <math>x\ne 0</math> we set <math>|x|_p=p^{-n}</math>, where {{mvar|n}} is the unique integer such that <math>x=p^n \frac{a}{b}</math> and ''a'' and ''b'' are two integers [[Coprime integers|coprime]] with ''p.''
*The ''p''-adic absolute value on the [[p-adic numbers|''p''-adic numbers]], arising from the completion (see {{section link|#Completions}} below) of the rationals with the absolute value defined above.
*If <math>F(x)</math> is the field of [[rational fraction]]s over a field {{math|''F''}} in the variable ''x'' and <math>P</math> is a fixed [[irreducible polynomial]] over {{math|''F''}}, the ''{{mvar|P}}-adic'' absolute value on <math>F(x)</math> is defined as follows: <math>|0|_P=0</math> and for <math>f\ne 0</math> we set <math>|f|_P=2^{-n},</math> where {{mvar|n}} is the unique integer such that <math display="inline">f = P^n \frac{G}{H},</math> where {{mvar|G}} and {{mvar|H}} are two polynomials, both [[Coprime polynomials|coprime]] with {{mvar|P}}.
*Absolute values are used to define or characterize [[global field|global]] and [[local field|local]] fields.

== Types of absolute value ==
The '''trivial''' absolute value is the absolute value with |''x''|&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 when ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 and |''x''|&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 otherwise.<ref>{{cite book |last=Koblitz |first=Neal |authorlink=Neal Koblitz |title=P-adic numbers, p-adic analysis, and zeta-functions |edition=2nd |year=1984 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-96017-3 |url=https://www.springer.com/mathematics/numbers/book/978-0-387-96017-3 |accessdate=24 August 2012 |page=3 |quote=By the 'trivial' norm we mean the norm&nbsp;‖&nbsp;‖ such that ‖0‖&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 and ‖''x''‖&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 for ''x''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0.}}</ref>  Every integral domain can carry at least the trivial absolute value. The trivial value is the only possible absolute value on a [[finite field]] because any non-zero element can be raised to some power to yield 1.

If an absolute value satisfies the stronger property |''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''|&nbsp;≤&nbsp;max(|''x''|,&nbsp;|''y''|) for all ''x'' and ''y'', then |''x''| is called an [[ultrametric]] or '''non-Archimedean absolute value''', and otherwise an '''Archimedean absolute value'''.

== Places ==
If |''x''|<sub>1</sub> and |''x''|<sub>2</sub> are two absolute values on the same integral domain ''D'', then the two absolute values are ''equivalent'' if |''x''|<sub>1</sub> < 1 [[if and only if]] |''x''|<sub>2</sub> < 1 for all ''x''. If two nontrivial absolute values are equivalent, then for some exponent ''e'' we have |''x''|<sub>1</sub><sup>''e''</sup> = |''x''|<sub>2</sub> for all ''x''. Raising an absolute value to a power less than 1 results in another absolute value, but raising to a power greater than 1 does not necessarily result in an absolute value. (For instance, squaring the usual absolute value on the real numbers yields a function which is not an absolute value because it violates the rule |''x''+''y''|&nbsp;≤&nbsp;|''x''|+|''y''|.) Absolute values up to equivalence, or in other words, an [[equivalence class]] of absolute values, is called a '''[[Algebraic number theory#Places|place]]'''.

Since the ordinary absolute value and the ''p''-adic absolute values are absolute values according to the definition above, these define places.

[[Ostrowski's theorem]] states that the nontrivial places of the [[rational numbers]] '''Q''' are the ordinary [[absolute value]] and the [[p-adic number|''p''-adic absolute value]] for each prime ''p''<ref>Cassels (1986) p.16</ref> (see the third example above).

== Valuations ==
{{main|Valuation (algebra)}}
If for some ultrametric absolute value and any base ''b''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, we define ''ν''(''x'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;−log<sub>''b''</sub>|''x''| for ''x''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0 and ''ν''(0)&nbsp;=&nbsp;∞, where ∞ is ordered to be greater than all real numbers, then we obtain a function from ''D'' to '''R'''&nbsp;∪&nbsp;{∞}, with the following properties:

* ''ν''(''x'') = ∞ ⇒ ''x'' = 0,
* ''ν''(''xy'') = ''ν''(''x'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;''ν''(''y''),
* ''ν''(''x'' + ''y'') ≥ min(ν(''x''), ''ν''(''y'')).

Such a function is known as a ''[[valuation (algebra)|valuation]]'' in the terminology of [[Nicolas Bourbaki|Bourbaki]], but other authors use the term ''valuation'' for ''absolute value'' and then say ''exponential valuation'' instead of ''valuation''.

== Completions ==
Given an integral domain ''D'' with an absolute value, we can define the [[Cauchy sequence]]s of elements of ''D'' with respect to the absolute value by requiring that for every ε&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 there is a positive integer ''N'' such that for all integers ''m'', ''n'' > ''N'' one has {{nowrap|&#124;''x''<sub>''m'' </sub> − ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>&#124; < ε.}} Cauchy sequences form a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] under pointwise addition and multiplication. One can also define null sequences as sequences (''a''<sub>''n''</sub>) of elements of ''D'' such that |''a''<sub>''n''</sub>| converges to zero. Null sequences are a [[prime ideal]] in the ring of Cauchy sequences, and the [[quotient ring]] is therefore an integral domain. The domain ''D'' is [[Embedding|embedded]] in this quotient ring, called the [[complete metric space|completion]] of ''D'' with respect to the absolute value |''x''|.

Since fields are integral domains, this is also a construction for the completion of a field with respect to an absolute value. To show that the result is a field, and not just an integral domain, we can either show that null sequences form a [[maximal ideal]], or else construct the inverse directly. The latter can be easily done by taking, for all nonzero elements of the quotient ring, a sequence starting from a point beyond the last zero element of the sequence. Any nonzero element of the quotient ring will differ by a null sequence from such a sequence, and by taking pointwise inversion we can find a representative inverse element.

Another theorem of [[Alexander Ostrowski]] has it that any field complete with respect to an [[Archimedes|Archimedean]] absolute value is [[isomorphic]] to either the real or the complex numbers, and the valuation is equivalent to the usual one.<ref>Cassels (1986) p.33</ref>  The '''Gelfand-Tornheim theorem''' states that any field with an Archimedean valuation is isomorphic to a [[Field extension|subfield]] of '''C''', the valuation being equivalent to the usual absolute value on '''C'''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.williamstein.org/papers/ant/html/node60.html |author=William Stein |title=Examples of Valuations |date=2004-05-06 |accessdate=2023-01-28 }}</ref>

== Fields and integral domains ==
If ''D'' is an integral domain with absolute value |''x''|, then we may extend the definition of the absolute value to the [[field of fractions]] of ''D'' by setting

:<math>|x/y| = |x|/|y|.\,</math>

On the other hand, if ''F'' is a field with ultrametric absolute value |''x''|, then the set of elements of ''F'' such that |''x''| ≤ 1 defines a [[valuation ring]], which is a [[subring]] ''D'' of ''F'' such that for every nonzero element ''x'' of ''F'', at least one of ''x'' or ''x''<sup>−1</sup> belongs to ''D''. Since ''F'' is a field, ''D'' has no [[zero divisor]]s and is an integral domain. It has a unique [[maximal ideal]] consisting of all ''x'' such that |''x''| < 1, and is therefore a [[local ring]].
